1210: Attached means joined to something or someone — physically, emotionally, or officially. The exact nature of that "joining" depends on the context, and the word carries several distinct but related meanings.
Meaning 1: Physically Fastened or Connected

The most literal meaning: something is attached when it is fixed to, connected to, or included with something else.

"Please read the attached file."
"The house has an attached garage."
"A label was attached to each box."

Here, "attached" simply tells you that one thing is joined to another — it isn't floating free on its own. An attached garage is built directly onto the house (unlike a detached garage, which stands separately). An attached file in an email is a document that comes along with the email, bundled to it.

The opposite in this sense is detached — meaning separated, disconnected, or standing alone.
Meaning 2: Emotionally Bonded (The Most Common Everyday Use)

This is the sense you'll encounter most often in daily life. When a person (or even an animal) is attached to someone or something, they have a strong emotional bond — a feeling of love, fondness, or deep connection that makes it hard to let go.

"She is very attached to her childhood home."
"The boy became deeply attached to his dog."
"He found it hard to leave — he had grown too attached."

This kind of attachment is about the heart, not the hands. You can be attached to:

  • A person (a parent, a friend, a partner)
  • A place (a hometown, an old house)
  • An object (a gift, a childhood toy)
  • An idea (a belief, a habit, a way of doing things)

Degrees of attachment matter:
The word scales in intensity. Compare:

  • "She's a little attached to her old phone." → mild fondness, reluctant to give it up
  • "He is deeply attached to his mother." → a strong, significant emotional bond
  • "She became unhealthily attached." → obsessive, difficult to separate from

The stronger the attachment, the harder it is to emotionally "detach." When someone is attached to a person or thing, losing it — even the thought of losing it — causes discomfort, sadness, or anxiety. That's the inner signal that attachment is present.

Attached vs. fond:
You might wonder: is "attached" just another word for being fond of something? Not quite. "Fond" means you like something. "Attached" goes a step further — it implies a kind of dependency or bond that makes separation difficult. You can be fond of a restaurant without being attached to it. But if you'd feel genuinely sad if it closed, you're attached.
Meaning 3: Already in a Romantic Relationship

In informal conversation, attached means a person is not romantically available — they are already in a relationship (dating someone, engaged, or married).

"Don't bother asking her out — she's attached."
"Are you single or attached?"

This usage comes directly from the emotional meaning: the person is already "bonded" to someone else. The opposite here is unattached — meaning single, free, not in a relationship.
Meaning 4: Officially Assigned or Appointed to a Group

In professional, military, or governmental contexts, attached means a person has been formally assigned to work with, or alongside, a particular unit, organization, or department — often temporarily, or in a supporting role.

"She was a journalist attached to the army."
"He worked as a diplomat attached to the embassy in Paris."
"The specialist was attached to the research team for three months."

Think of it as being "plugged in" to a group for an official purpose. The person isn't a permanent member — they've been connected to it for a specific role or period. This sense is most common in formal, official, or news contexts.
Meaning 5: Seized by Legal Authority (formal/legal)

In legal language, attached can describe property or assets that have been officially seized by a court or legal authority — taken away from someone as part of a legal proceeding, often to satisfy a debt or judgment.

"His assets were attached by court order."

You'll mainly see this in legal documents and formal writing. It's a narrow, specialized use — but good to know so you're not confused if you encounter it.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Intended

Context is everything. Ask yourself: what kind of thing is "attached" here?

ContextMeaning
A file, a document, a building, a labelPhysically connected
A person feeling something about another person, place, or objectEmotional bond
A person's relationship statusRomantically taken
A person's role in an official bodyAssigned/appointed
Property in a legal caseSeized by law
  • If a file or object is attached → it is physically joined or included.
  • If a person feels attached → it is an emotional bond.
  • If someone describes another person as attached in conversation about romance → they are in a relationship.
  • If a person is described as attached to an organization in a professional context → they've been assigned there.
  • If property is described as attached in a legal setting → it has been seized.
The Underlying Thread

Notice that all these meanings share a single thread: a connection that holds things together. Whether it's a file clipped to an email, a child who can't bear to leave their parent, a diplomat serving at an embassy, or a garage joined to a house — in every case, "attached" means not free-floating, not separate, but bound to something else.

The word carries a subtle implication: because of this connection, separation is either impossible, difficult, or officially restricted.
The Opposite: Detached

The natural antonym of attached is detached. And just like "attached," it works on all the same levels:

  • A detached house stands alone (not joined to another).
  • A detached person feels no strong emotional bond — they are emotionally distant, uninvested, or indifferent.
  • Someone who approaches a problem with detached thinking is calm, rational, and unaffected by personal feelings.

Understanding "detached" sharpens your grasp of "attached" — they define each other.
Common Phrases and Collocations

These are the word combinations you'll most often see or hear:

  • Attached to — the most common pattern: "attached to a person," "attached to an idea," "attached to the wall"
  • Become attached — the process of forming a bond: "She slowly became attached to him."
  • Deeply / strongly / emotionally attached — intensifiers that show the bond is powerful
  • Overly attached — used when the bond is excessive or unhealthy
  • Please find attached — a formal phrase used in emails or letters to point to an enclosed document: "Please find attached the report you requested."
  • Attached herewith / attached hereto — very formal or legal versions of the same idea
  • No strings attached — a common expression meaning something is given freely, with no obligations or conditions tied to it (using "attached" metaphorically to mean conditions or expectations)
A Final Note on the Emotional Sense

Of all the meanings, the emotional sense is the richest and most worth understanding deeply, because it touches something universal.

Attachment is neither purely good nor purely bad — it depends on its nature and intensity. A healthy attachment to a loved one is the foundation of meaningful relationships. An unhealthy or excessive attachment — where you cannot function without a person or thing, or where loss causes disproportionate suffering — is what psychologists call unhealthy attachment or dependency.

When someone says "try not to get too attached," they're gently warning you not to form a bond so strong that you'll be hurt when things change — because things always do. The advice is about emotional protection, not coldness.

That is the word attached — in all its forms, shades, and situations.

Imagine you are a baby. You cannot feed yourself, protect yourself, or even move very far on your own. Your survival depends entirely on another person — usually a parent. So your brain, from the very first days of life, is wired to do one critical thing: bond with that person, stay close to them, and use them as a safe refuge.

That bond — the emotional connection between a child and their caregiver — is called an attachment. And the entire body of scientific knowledge about how that bond forms, what shapes it, and how it affects the rest of your life is called attachment theory.

Attachment theory says: the way you were cared for in early childhood shapes a lifelong blueprint inside your mind — a blueprint that quietly governs how you relate to other people, how you handle emotions, and how safe or unsafe love feels to you.

Attachment theory was developed by a British psychiatrist named John Bowlby in the 1950s and 60s. Bowlby was working with emotionally troubled children and noticed something striking: children who were separated from their mothers — especially in early childhood — suffered profound psychological damage, even when all their physical needs (food, shelter, warmth) were fully met.

This was a revolutionary idea at the time. The mainstream belief was that a child's love for their mother was simply about food — the mother feeds you, so you "attach" to her as a kind of habit. Bowlby disagreed fundamentally. He argued that the need for emotional closeness and connection is a biological drive in its own right — just as powerful and primal as hunger or thirst. You don't bond with your caregiver because they feed you. You need the bond itself. Feeding is just one context in which the bond is expressed.

Later, a psychologist named Mary Ainsworth took Bowlby's ideas and tested them in the real world. Her research in the 1970s — particularly a famous experiment called the "Strange Situation" — gave us the first scientific map of different attachment styles. A third researcher, Mary Main, extended this work further in the 1980s and 90s, especially into how attachment plays out in adult life.
The Core Idea: The Secure Base

Bowlby introduced a concept that is central to understanding everything else: the secure base.

Think about a toddler at a playground. They will run around, explore, try things, take small risks — but every so often, they glance back at their parent. Or they run back for a hug before darting off again. The parent is their secure base: a safe, reliable anchor from which the child feels free to explore the world.

When something scary happens — a loud noise, a stranger, a fall — the child immediately runs back to the caregiver. The caregiver soothes them. Once calmed, the child ventures out again. This pattern — explore, get scared, return, get comforted, explore again — is the engine of healthy development.

A child with a dependable secure base learns two enormously important things:

  1. The world is safe enough to explore.
  2. When things go wrong, other people can be trusted to help me.

A child without a reliable secure base learns the opposite — and carries that lesson into every relationship for the rest of their life, unless something changes it.
Internal Working Models: The Blueprint in Your Mind

Here is where it gets really interesting. Bowlby said that based on their early experiences with caregivers, children build a kind of mental model — a subconscious template or blueprint — of how relationships work. He called these internal working models.

This mental model has two sides:

  • A model of others: Are people trustworthy? Will they be there when I need them? Do people generally care about me?
  • A model of self: Am I worthy of love? Am I someone whose needs matter? Am I capable?

A child whose caregiver consistently responds to their needs warmly and reliably builds a model that says: "People are trustworthy. I am lovable. When I need help, I can ask for it and it will come."

A child whose caregiver is cold, unpredictable, or absent builds a different model: "People cannot be relied on. I may not be worthy of care. It is safer to manage on my own — or to cling desperately and never let go."

Here is the crucial part: these models don't stay locked in childhood. They follow you. They shape how you behave in friendships, romantic relationships, and even at work. They influence whether you trust a partner or constantly suspect they'll leave. They determine whether you can ask for help or feel ashamed for needing it. They color your emotional life in ways you may not even consciously notice.

Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation experiment involved placing a child briefly in an unfamiliar room with a stranger, then having the parent leave, and then watching how the child reacted when the parent returned. What she observed led to the identification of distinct patterns of attachment. Later researchers added a fourth. Here they are:

1. Secure Attachment

This develops when a caregiver is consistently warm, responsive, and available. When the child is upset, the caregiver soothes them reliably. The caregiver doesn't need to be perfect — just "good enough" and dependable.

In the experiment: The child was distressed when the parent left (which is normal and healthy), but when the parent returned, the child quickly calmed down, accepted comfort, and went back to playing. They used the parent as exactly what they were supposed to be: a safe haven.

What this child learns: People can be trusted. My emotions are manageable. Relationships are a source of comfort, not danger.

In adult life: Securely attached adults tend to find relationships fulfilling rather than terrifying. They can be intimate without losing themselves. They can handle conflict without catastrophizing. They can ask for help without shame and give it without resentment. They don't constantly fear being abandoned or smothered. Roughly 55-65% of people in most studied populations show secure attachment — it is the most common style.

2. Anxious (Ambivalent) Attachment

This develops when the caregiver is inconsistent — sometimes warm and responsive, sometimes distracted, unavailable, or intrusive. The child can never quite predict which version of the parent they'll get.

In the experiment: The child was extremely distressed when the parent left — far more than expected. When the parent returned, the child didn't calm down easily. They were angry, clingy, and couldn't settle — sometimes hitting the parent or pushing them away while simultaneously reaching for them. It was as if they wanted comfort but couldn't trust it.

What this child learns: I have to work very hard to get love. If I let my guard down, the person might disappear. I need to stay hypervigilant to threats to the relationship.

In adult life: Anxiously attached adults tend to worry a great deal about relationships. They may crave intimacy intensely but then feel smothered, or feel deeply insecure and need constant reassurance. Small signals — a delayed text message, a partner seeming distracted — can trigger intense anxiety. They may come across as "needy" or "clingy," but what is actually happening is that their nervous system was trained to be on high alert for signs of abandonment. This style is often called preoccupied attachment in adults.

3. Avoidant Attachment

This develops when the caregiver is emotionally unavailable, cold, or dismissive of the child's emotional needs. The parent may be physically present but emotionally distant. When the child cries or reaches for comfort, the caregiver pulls back, ignores it, or even shows mild irritation.

In the experiment: The child seemed almost unaffected when the parent left — which looked like independence. But this was deceptive. When researchers measured stress hormones, these children were just as internally distressed as others. They had simply learned to suppress the outward expression of their distress, because expressing it had never gotten them any help.

What this child learns: Showing emotion and needing others leads nowhere — or makes things worse. The safest strategy is to be self-sufficient and keep emotions at arm's length.

In adult life: Avoidantly attached adults value independence intensely and often feel uncomfortable with emotional intimacy. They may pull away when a relationship gets serious. They might say they don't "need" anyone, or feel vaguely suffocated when a partner wants to get close. This doesn't mean they don't have feelings or want connection — it means their brain learned very early that depending on others is risky, and that emotions are better suppressed than expressed. This style is often called dismissive-avoidant attachment in adults.

4. Disorganized Attachment

This was identified later by researcher Mary Main and is the most complex and painful of the four. It develops when the caregiver is the source of both comfort and fear — typically in situations involving abuse, severe neglect, or a caregiver who is themselves deeply traumatized and behaves in frightening or confusing ways.

This creates a fundamental impossibility for the child: their biology drives them toward their caregiver for safety, but their caregiver is also the source of danger. The child's attachment system has no coherent strategy to follow. It is like a computer running two contradictory programs at once — it freezes.

In the experiment: The child showed confused, contradictory behavior — running toward the parent, then stopping and falling to the floor, or reaching for the parent while turning their face away, or momentarily "spacing out."

In adult life: Disorganized attachment in adults (sometimes called fearful-avoidant) often manifests as wanting closeness desperately while also fearing it intensely. These individuals may swing between craving intimacy and pushing people away. They often struggle with emotional regulation, trust, and identity. This style is strongly linked to early trauma and is frequently observed in adults who have experienced chaotic or abusive childhoods.

A common misconception is that attachment theory only applies to babies and young children. It does not. Bowlby always insisted that attachment behavior is active "from the cradle to the grave."

As we grow up, our primary attachment figures shift. In childhood it is parents. In adolescence it may be close friends. In adulthood it becomes romantic partners — who take on the full role of attachment figure for most people: the person you turn to when you are sick, scared, or in pain; the person whose absence causes the most distress; the person in whose presence you feel most at ease.

This is why your attachment style shows up so vividly in romantic relationships. A relationship with a partner is not just emotionally important — it activates the same deep biological system that kept you alive as an infant. The stakes feel enormous because, evolutionarily speaking, they once were.

Your internal working model was built through thousands of repeated experiences in early childhood. It became deeply encoded — not as a conscious belief you chose, but as an automatic, subconscious way of interpreting and responding to the world.

Furthermore, your attachment style tends to be self-reinforcing. An anxiously attached person, frightened of abandonment, may behave in ways (clinging, constant reassurance-seeking, jealousy) that eventually pushes partners away — which then confirms their belief that people always leave. An avoidantly attached person who keeps emotional distance may attract partners who feel shut out and eventually give up — which confirms their belief that depending on others is foolish. The blueprint doesn't just predict your relationships; it can actively shape them.

Yes. This is one of the most hopeful findings in this field. Your attachment style is not a life sentence.

Attachment styles can change through:

New relationships. A consistently warm, patient, and reliable romantic partner can gradually help rewrite your internal working model. This is sometimes called "earned security" — you develop secure attachment not from a perfect childhood, but from corrective experiences later in life.

Therapy. A skilled therapist essentially provides a secure base in the therapeutic relationship itself. You experience a relationship where someone is consistently present, non-judgmental, and attuned — often for the first time. Over time, this can shift deep-seated patterns. Therapies like Emotionally Focused Therapy (EFT) are specifically built around attachment principles.

Self-awareness. Simply understanding your attachment style — knowing why you react the way you do, recognizing when your nervous system is responding to a past threat rather than a present one — can create enough distance from automatic patterns to begin changing them.

Research suggests that around 25% of adults who started life with insecure attachment develop what is called "earned secure attachment" through these kinds of experiences.

Attachment theory is not just an interesting piece of psychology trivia. It has profound practical implications:

For parenting: You don't need to be a perfect parent — you need to be a "good enough" one. Responsiveness matters more than technique. Repair matters — when you mess up (and all parents do), the act of reconnecting and soothing the child is itself a powerful attachment-building moment.

For relationships: Understanding your attachment style explains patterns you may have noticed in yourself but couldn't account for — why you panic when a partner is distant, why you shut down during arguments, why intimacy feels threatening, or why you feel compelled to be completely self-sufficient.

For mental health: Insecure attachment is strongly linked to anxiety disorders, depression, difficulties with emotion regulation, and vulnerability to trauma. Many of the struggles people bring to therapy are, at their root, attachment wounds.

For society: The quality of early caregiving has consequences that ripple outward — into schools, workplaces, communities, and the next generation of parents. A society that supports caregivers is investing in the psychological foundations of its future population.
A Final Summary to Tie It All Together

Attachment theory, in its entirety, rests on a few powerful ideas:

First, humans are biologically wired to form deep emotional bonds, and this need for connection is a primary drive — not a luxury or a byproduct of something else.

Second, the quality of your earliest bonds — particularly with your primary caregiver — shapes a subconscious blueprint (an internal working model) that tells you whether people are trustworthy, whether you are worthy of love, and whether the world is safe enough to explore.

Third, this blueprint expresses itself as an attachment style — secure, anxious, avoidant, or disorganized — which quietly governs how you relate to others throughout your life.

Fourth, while early experiences are profoundly influential, they are not destiny. With the right relationships, insight, or support, the blueprint can be rewritten.

In short: who you are in relationships reflects, in large part, who first held you — and how. But it also reflects every meaningful relationship since then, and every meaningful one still to come.

An attaché is a specialist official who is attached — that is, assigned and connected — to a diplomatic mission, such as an embassy or consulate, in a foreign country. Think of an embassy as a team sent by one country to live and work inside another country. Most of that team handles general diplomacy, but some members are brought in specifically because they have deep expertise in a particular field. Those specialists are called attachés.

The word essentially means: "a person officially attached to a larger body for a specific purpose."
Where They Work and Who They Represent

An attaché represents their home country while stationed abroad. So an Indian military attaché posted in Washington D.C. is an Indian official working inside India's embassy in America, and their job is specifically to handle military-related matters between the two countries.

They are always part of a larger diplomatic mission — they don't operate independently. The embassy is the team; the attaché is a specialist player on that team.

The key quality is specialization. A general diplomat handles broad political and diplomatic work. An attaché is different — they are there because they have expert knowledge in one particular domain (military affairs, trade, culture, science, etc.). Their entire role within the embassy is focused on that domain.

Because the word simply describes "a specialist assigned to an embassy," there are many types depending on the field:

Military Attaché
The most well-known type. This is a military officer (often from the army, navy, or air force) who serves at an embassy. Their job is to observe and report on the military capabilities, activities, and policies of the host country, and to maintain official military communication between the two nations. You'll sometimes hear more specific titles like army attaché, naval attaché, or air attaché. A defense attaché or defence attaché is a senior officer who oversees all the military branches' attachés at a given embassy.

Commercial Attaché / Trade Attaché
This person focuses on trade and business. They help companies from their home country do business in the foreign country, report on local markets, and work to build trade relationships between the two nations.

Cultural Attaché
They handle the cultural relationship between the two countries — things like promoting their home country's art, language, literature, and education in the foreign land. For example, they might organize film festivals, support language programs, or facilitate academic exchanges.

Press Attaché / Media Attaché
This person manages the embassy's relationship with journalists and the media in the host country. They act as a spokesperson, issue press releases, and control the flow of official information to the press.

Science and Technology Attaché
Found at some embassies, this person focuses on scientific cooperation and technology exchange between the two nations.
The Rank Question: Are They Senior or Junior?

Traditionally, the title "attaché" without any other word in front of it referred to a junior diplomatic officer — often someone early in their career, learning the ropes of diplomacy. This is still a valid usage. In a formal diplomatic ranking list, a plain attaché sits near the bottom, below a third secretary, second secretary, first secretary, counsellor, and so on up to the ambassador.

However, when the word is used with a specialty in front of it (like military attaché or commercial attaché), it doesn't necessarily imply a junior rank at all — a military attaché, for instance, is often a senior officer, sometimes a colonel or brigadier.

So the meaning shifts slightly:

  • Attaché (alone) → a junior-level diplomat
  • [Field] + attaché → a specialist of any seniority in that field

The word is also used for a specific type of bag — the slim, hard-sided, rectangular briefcase that professionals carry. It's called an attaché case (sometimes shortened in common speech to just "an attaché"). The name comes from the fact that these bags were historically associated with diplomats and attachés, who carried documents and official papers in them. Today the term is used for any similar-looking flat, rigid briefcase, whether or not the owner is a diplomat.
How It's Used in Real Sentences

• "The French ambassador introduced her team, including the military attaché and the cultural attaché."
  • "He started his diplomatic career as a junior attaché at the embassy in Cairo."
  • "The defense attaché filed a detailed report on the joint military exercise."
  • "She snapped open her leather attaché case and removed the documents."
  • "The trade attaché helped local businesses navigate export procedures."
A Simple Way to Remember It

Picture an embassy as a building full of diplomats. Now imagine that inside that building, there's a room full of specialists — a general, a trade expert, a journalist-handler, a culture promoter. Each of those specialists, formally assigned there in an official capacity, is an attaché. They are attached to the mission, contributing their expertise to the larger diplomatic effort.

An attack is a sudden, aggressive, or forceful action directed at a target — with the aim of harming, defeating, damaging, or overcoming it. The target can be a person, a place, an idea, a body, or even a problem.

Think of it this way: whenever something comes at something else with force or intensity, that is an attack.

1. Physical violence against a person

This is the most basic and common meaning. An attack happens when one person (or a group) uses physical force to hurt another.

  • The man was the victim of a violent attack on his way home.
  • The dog's attack left the child injured.

Notice that the word "attack" here focuses on the event of violence — the act itself. It doesn't tell you whether the attacker succeeded or not; it just names what happened.

2. A military or armed strike

In warfare, an attack is an organized, deliberate offensive action — when soldiers, aircraft, ships, or weapons are used to strike at an enemy position, base, or force.

  • The army launched a surprise attack at midnight.
  • The city survived the air attack with minimal damage.
  • The enemy's attack was repelled after hours of fighting.

Here the word suggests careful planning combined with violent force. A military attack has a target, a direction, and usually a goal (to capture territory, destroy a base, or weaken the enemy).

3. A verbal or written assault (criticism)

You don't need physical weapons to "attack" someone. When someone strongly and aggressively criticizes a person, an institution, or an idea — especially in public — that too is called an attack.

  • The journalist's attack on the politician was published on the front page.
  • Her speech was a fierce attack on the government's handling of the crisis.
  • The review was less a critique and more a personal attack on the author.

The key here is that the criticism is forceful, aggressive, and intended to damage — not mild or friendly. An ordinary disagreement is not an attack; an attack is fierce and feels hostile.

4. A sudden episode of illness or a medical condition

In health and medicine, an attack refers to a sudden, unexpected, and often severe episode of a particular condition. It comes on quickly, without much warning, and can be frightening or dangerous.

  • He clutched his chest — it was a heart attack.
  • She had to sit down during the panic attack; her heart was racing.
  • The child's asthma attack was triggered by the cold air.
  • He had an epileptic attack in the middle of the meeting.

The word "attack" is used here because the condition comes at the person suddenly and forcefully, almost like an enemy — they didn't invite it, and it overwhelms them for a period of time.

Common medical attacks:

  • Heart attack — a sudden blockage of blood supply to the heart
  • Panic attack — a sudden wave of intense fear and physical symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness)
  • Asthma attack — a sudden tightening of the airways, making breathing difficult
  • Epileptic attack — a sudden episode of uncontrolled electrical activity in the brain (a seizure)
  • Anxiety attack — a sudden surge of intense anxiety and distress
  • Migraine attack — a sudden, severe episode of headache with other symptoms

5. A sudden, overwhelming feeling or urge

Related to the medical meaning, this is when you are suddenly and powerfully overcome by a feeling or sensation — usually something you didn't expect or can't easily control.

  • She had an attack of the giggles and couldn't stop laughing.
  • He was struck by a sudden attack of guilt after lying to her.
  • An attack of nerves before the performance left him trembling.

This usage is slightly informal, but very natural in everyday English. It treats the feeling as something that "comes at you" from the outside, even though it comes from within.

6. A forceful, determined effort to deal with a problem

When someone tackles a difficult task or problem with great energy, focus, and determination, you can call it an attack.

  • The team made an energetic attack on the mountain of paperwork.
  • His attack on the math problem was systematic and thorough.

This meaning is less about violence and more about intensity and commitment. It borrows the energy of the word without the hostility.

7. In sport: offensive play or the attacking players

In many sports (football, hockey, chess, basketball), an attack refers to an offensive move — the team or player moving toward the opponent's goal or position.

  • The team's attack in the second half was unstoppable.
  • The chess player launched a fierce attack on the opponent's king.
  • The winger broke through the defense in a lightning attack.

Sometimes "the attack" refers collectively to the forward or offensive players on a team:

  • Their attack scored three goals in ten minutes. (meaning: the forwards, the offensive players)

8. In music: the start of a note

This is a technical, specialized meaning. In music, the "attack" of a note means how a sound begins — how quickly and sharply it rises from silence to full volume.

  • The violinist had a clean, crisp attack on each note.
  • A softer attack gives the music a more gentle, flowing feel.

This is a term mainly used by musicians, sound engineers, and music teachers, but it's worth knowing.

Attack vs. fight vs. assault

These words are related but not identical.

  • A fight suggests two sides engaging each other roughly equally.
  • An assault is a legal and often physical term — it implies direct bodily harm or the serious threat of it.
  • An attack is broader and more general — it can be physical, verbal, medical, or metaphorical, and it doesn't require both sides to be fighting back.

"Under attack"

This phrase means you are currently being targeted by an attack — you are the victim or the target.

  • The village was under attack.
  • The minister's reputation came under attack from all sides.

"Launch / mount an attack"

To launch or mount an attack means to begin or carry out an attack.

  • The rebels launched an attack before dawn.
  • Critics mounted a fierce attack on the proposal.

"Repel / withstand / survive an attack"

These phrases mean to successfully defend yourself against an attack.

  • The defenders repelled every attack.
  • The bridge withstood the attack.

"An attack on something"

An attack is almost always directed at a specific target. You will often see the preposition on following the noun:

  • an attack on the embassy
  • an attack on her character
  • an attack on the problem

Across all these different contexts — war, medicine, sport, criticism, and everyday life — the word attack carries the same essential character:

Something comes suddenly, with force or intensity, directed at a target, intending to harm, defeat, or overwhelm it.

Whether it's soldiers storming a fort, a virus overwhelming the immune system, a critic tearing apart a book, or a person bursting into uncontrollable laughter — when something strikes with suddenness and force, English calls it an attack.

To attain something means to successfully reach or achieve something — especially after putting in effort, time, or going through a process to get there.

Think of it like climbing a mountain. You don't just get to the top — you work your way up and finally arrive. That moment of finally arriving at something meaningful, after a journey of effort, is what "attain" captures.

She attained the highest rank in her field after decades of dedicated work.

The word carries two ideas at the same time:

  1. Arrival — you have reached something (a goal, a level, a state, a position)
  2. Effort — it didn't happen by accident; there was a process involved

This is why "attain" is never used for small, easy, or accidental things. You wouldn't say "I attained a sandwich for lunch." You use it for things that are significant and worth noting — things like mastery, success, wisdom, freedom, a status, or an important milestone.
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

1. To achieve a goal or reach a desired outcome

This is about accomplishing something you were working toward — a dream, an objective, a standard.

He finally attained his goal of running a marathon.
The country attained its independence after a long struggle.
She worked tirelessly to attain perfection in her craft.

2. To reach a particular level, age, state, or degree

Here, "attain" is used when something or someone reaches a measurable or definable point — a temperature, an age, a speed, a rank, a condition.

The rocket attained a speed of 25,000 kilometers per hour.
He attained the age of 100 in remarkable health.
The water attained its boiling point.
The student attained an advanced level of proficiency.

Notice that in this second use, it doesn't always imply personal struggle — a rocket doesn't "try" to go fast — but it still describes the act of reaching a significant, defined point.

It does not mean:

  • Simply getting or receiving something passively (that would be "obtain" or "receive")
  • Doing or completing a task (that would be "accomplish")
  • Trying but not yet succeeding (it only describes successful arrival)

"Attain" is always about having successfully arrived at something. It looks back at a completed journey, not forward at an attempt.
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words often feel similar, but here is what sets each apart:

  • Achieve — Very close to "attain," but achieve puts the spotlight on the accomplishment itself. Attain puts the spotlight on reaching a level or standard. You achieve a victory; you attain mastery. (Often interchangeable, but this is the subtle difference.)
  • Reach — More neutral and physical. Reach can simply mean to extend your hand and touch something. Attain is more formal and always implies something meaningful being gained.
  • Obtain — Means to get or acquire something, usually something physical or concrete (a document, a permit, a copy of something). Attain is about reaching a state or level, not just getting an object.
  • Accomplish — Means to complete or carry out a specific task. Accomplish is about finishing something. Attain is about arriving somewhere — a status, a quality, a condition.
Common Combinations (What "Attain" Is Often Paired With)

"Attain" is almost always followed by an abstract or significant noun. Here are the most natural pairings:

  • attain a goal / an objective / a dream
  • attain success / mastery / excellence / perfection
  • attain wisdom / enlightenment / peace
  • attain freedom / independence / justice
  • attain a level / a standard / a rank / a position / a status
  • attain the age of [number]
  • attain a speed / a temperature (in technical or scientific writing)
Register: When Do People Use This Word?

"Attain" is a formal word. You will see and hear it most in:

  • Academic writing and textbooks
  • Professional or business contexts
  • Literary or philosophical writing
  • Formal speeches or official documents

In everyday casual conversation, people tend to use simpler words like "reach," "get," "achieve," or "make it to" instead. For example, a friend would likely say "She finally got the promotion" rather than "She attained the promotion" — even though the second is grammatically correct.

This means if you use "attain" in your writing or formal speech, it will sound intelligent, precise, and elevated. Just avoid using it in casual texting or small talk, where it will sound unnatural.

• Attain is always a transitive verb — it must always be followed by an object. You cannot say "She finally attained" and stop there. You must say what was attained: "She finally attained her goal."
  • It works in passive voice too:

The goal was finally attained after years of hard work.
Financial stability was attained through careful planning.

  • The noun form is attainment (the act or result of attaining something):

The attainment of wisdom takes a lifetime.
Educational attainment is measured across the country.
One-Line Summary to Remember It By

"Attain" means to successfully arrive at something significant — a goal, a level, a state, or a milestone — after effort or a process.

Every time you see or use this word, picture someone finally reaching the top of a long climb — not by luck, but by deliberate effort — and standing there, having truly arrived.
1215:
"Attainment" has two closely connected meanings that work together:

The first is the act or process of successfully reaching something — a goal, a level, a standard — especially after putting in real effort over time. The second is the thing itself that has been reached — a skill, an ability, a level of knowledge, a position.

Think of climbing a mountain. The long, hard climb is the attainment (the process), and standing at the summit is also your attainment (the thing achieved). Both ideas live in the same word.
The key idea the word carries

"Attainment" always implies that something of real value was reached, not by accident or luck, but through sustained effort, discipline, or growth. This is an important feature of the word. You would never use it for something trivial or accidental. Finding a coin on the street is not an attainment. Earning a medical degree after a decade of hard study very much is.
Where you will commonly see this word

The most frequent use is in education. "Educational attainment" refers to the level of education someone has successfully reached — whether that's finishing high school, earning a university degree, or reaching a certain academic standard. You will see this phrase constantly in news articles, government reports, and academic writing.

Beyond education, the word appears wherever someone has successfully reached something meaningful: the attainment of knowledge, the attainment of financial independence, the attainment of inner peace, the attainment of a high professional position. It works naturally with both concrete goals and abstract ones.

"Her educational attainment gave her access to opportunities she never had before." (= the level of education she successfully reached)

"The attainment of financial freedom took him fifteen years of disciplined saving." (= the act of successfully reaching that goal)

"Speaking three languages fluently is a remarkable attainment." (= a remarkable thing she has achieved)

"The new policy aims to raise student attainment across all schools." (= the level of academic achievement students reach)

"After years of practice, mastering the violin felt like his greatest attainment." (= the most valuable thing he had ever successfully achieved)

This is a formal word. You will encounter it mostly in written, academic, or official contexts — educational research, policy documents, formal speeches, self-development books. In everyday casual conversation, people are far more likely to say "achievement" or "accomplishment." Knowing this helps you understand when and where to use it.

Achievement is the closest word and the two overlap heavily. The main difference is that "achievement" is versatile — used in both formal and informal settings, and it often points to a specific thing done successfully. "Attainment" feels broader and more formal, and tends to suggest reaching a level or standard rather than completing one particular task.

Accomplishment often refers to a specific completed act, or a talent a person possesses. You might say someone is a person of many accomplishments, listing specific things they've done. "Attainment" feels more like arriving at a destination after a long journey.

Acquisition is about getting or obtaining something — especially knowledge or skills — while "attainment" is about the reaching of a level or goal. "Language acquisition" describes the process of picking up a language; "language attainment" describes what level of that language a person has successfully reached.

It does not mean an attempt. You only use this word when the goal has actually been reached, not merely tried. It also does not describe anything that happened passively or by chance — attainment always involves deliberate effort or growth.

When used in plural, "attainments" refers to a collection of skills, abilities, or achievements a person has built up. For example: "His attainments included fluency in four languages, a doctorate in physics, and an internationally recognized body of research." This usage is somewhat formal and old-fashioned but still appears in writing, especially when describing a distinguished person's range of abilities.
A simple way to remember it
If you reach something valuable through real effort — and you actually get there — that is attainment. The word captures both the journey of getting there and the prize of having arrived.
1216:
An attempt is an act of trying to do something. That's the heart of it. When someone makes an attempt, they put in effort toward a goal — but the key thing is: the result is not certain. They might succeed, or they might fail.

Think of it this way: the word "attempt" lives in the space between starting and succeeding. It describes the act of trying, not the outcome.

She made an attempt to open the jar, but it was too tight.

She tried. She put in effort. But it didn't work. That whole action — the trying — is the attempt.

Many words describe doing something. "Attempt" is different because it specifically describes trying to do something where failure is possible, and often expected.

You wouldn't normally say:

"He made an attempt to breathe."

Because breathing (for a healthy person) is automatic and effortless — failure isn't really on the table. But you would say:

"He made an attempt to climb the mountain."

Because climbing a mountain is hard, uncertain, and you might not make it.

So "attempt" carries a built-in sense of difficulty and uncertainty. The moment you call something an attempt, you are quietly admitting: this was not easy, and success was not guaranteed.

This is the most important thing to understand. An attempt can succeed or fail, but the word by itself does not tell you which one happened. You have to look at the context.

His first attempt failed. His second attempt succeeded.

Both sentences use "attempt" correctly. The word is neutral about the outcome — it only tells you that trying happened.

However — and this is a subtle but important point — in everyday use, people tend to use "attempt" more often when things don't quite go as planned. If someone successfully does something easily, they usually just say they did it, not that they made an attempt. The word subtly suggests struggle, even when it doesn't technically require it.
A Special Meaning: An Attack on Someone's Life

There is one specific, serious context where "attempt" has a narrower and more dramatic meaning:

An attempt on someone's life

This phrase means an act of trying to kill someone. It's formal and often appears in news, history, or legal contexts.

There was an attempt on the president's life.

This means someone tried to assassinate (kill) the president. Notice the word "on" here — attempt on a life is a fixed, well-known phrase. You wouldn't replace "on" with another word in this context.

When using "attempt" as a noun, it connects to the rest of the sentence in two main ways:

1. attempt + to + verb
This is used when you want to say what the person was trying to do.

She made an attempt to escape.
They made an attempt to fix the problem.
His attempt to apologize was awkward but sincere.

2. attempt + at + noun/gerund (-ing verb)
This is used when the thing being tried is expressed as a noun or a noun-like form.

It was a poor attempt at humor.
He made a brave attempt at speaking French.
Her attempt at the world record was impressive.

Both patterns are correct. The choice depends simply on what follows the word — a verb or a noun.

Make an attempt — the most natural way to use this noun; "make" is the go-to verb with "attempt."

Please make an attempt to arrive on time.

A failed/unsuccessful attempt — when the try didn't work out.

After several failed attempts, he finally gave up.

A successful attempt — when the try did work out.

It was the first successful attempt to reach the summit in winter.

A desperate attempt — when someone tries with urgency, often as a last resort.

She made a desperate attempt to catch the falling vase.

In an attempt to... — a very common phrase used to explain why someone did something.

He worked through the night in an attempt to finish the project.
She smiled in an attempt to hide her nervousness.

This last phrase is extremely useful in writing. It shows motivation or purpose behind an action.

"Attempt" is a countable noun, which means you can count individual attempts.

one attempt, two attempts, several attempts, many attempts

This matters because it shows that each try is seen as a separate, distinct event.

He passed the exam on his third attempt. (He tried twice before and failed.)

Here are a few rich example sentences that show the word in action across different contexts:

The team's attempt to break the world record fell just short — they finished three seconds too slow.

It was a clumsy attempt at a joke, and nobody laughed.

In an attempt to save money, they stopped eating out entirely.

Despite repeated attempts, the door wouldn't budge.

Historians believe there were at least two attempts on the king's life before he died of natural causes.
An attempt is the act of trying to do something difficult or uncertain — it says that effort was made, but makes no promise about whether it worked.
1217:
When you attempt something, you try to do it — but with a very important detail baked in: you are not sure you will succeed. There is a real possibility of failure, and you know it. You are making an effort toward a goal that is uncertain, difficult, or challenging.

That is the heart of the word. It is not just trying something casually. It carries a sense of deliberate effort against some difficulty or risk.
Breaking It Down with Simple Examples

She attempted to climb the mountain.

This tells you she put in real effort to climb it. But it does not tell you she reached the top. She may have succeeded, or she may have failed. The word "attempted" covers both possibilities — it only promises the effort, not the result.

Compare that to:

She climbed the mountain.

Now you know she succeeded. The action is complete and confirmed.

This contrast shows you something important: "attempt" focuses on the effort and the trying, not on whether the goal was achieved.

You would not normally say "I attempted to breathe" or "I attempted to blink." That would sound strange, because breathing and blinking are effortless — there is no real chance of failing at them.

"Attempt" naturally fits situations where:

  • The task is hard or demanding.
  • The outcome is uncertain.
  • There is a real chance of failing.
  • You are doing something brave, risky, or ambitious.

The scientist attempted to find a cure for the disease.
The student attempted every question on the exam, even the hardest ones.
He attempted to fix the broken engine, though he had no experience.
The negotiators attempted to reach a peace agreement.

In all of these, there is effort, there is difficulty, and the outcome is not guaranteed.

"Attempt" as a verb is used in two main ways:

1. Attempt + to + verb (infinitive)
This is the most common pattern.

She attempted to solve the puzzle.
They attempted to escape from the building.
He attempted to speak calmly, but his voice shook.

2. Attempt + a noun (a thing)
Here you attempt an action or task that is named as a noun.

She attempted the challenge.
He attempted the jump.
The team attempted a comeback in the final minutes.
She attempted an apology, but the words came out wrong.

Both patterns are correct. The first is more common in everyday use; the second is slightly more compact and often found in writing.
"Attempt" vs. "Try" — What Is the Real Difference?

These two words are close in meaning, and in many sentences, you can use either one. But there are subtle differences worth knowing.

"Try" is the everyday, neutral word. It is informal, versatile, and fits almost any situation — big or small, easy or hard.

Try the soup. Try turning it off and on again. Try to relax.

"Attempt" is more formal and more serious. It tends to be used when:

  • The task is more significant, difficult, or ambitious.
  • The context is professional, academic, legal, or official.
  • You want to emphasize deliberate, conscious effort.
  • The possibility of failure feels more real or more weighty.

The surgeon attempted a complex procedure that had never been done before.
(More natural than: The surgeon tried a complex procedure... — though "tried" still works.)

Please attempt all questions in Section B.
(Formal instruction, as on an exam paper.)

He attempted to deceive the court.
(Legal or serious context — sounds more precise and grave than "He tried to deceive the court," though both are grammatically correct.)

In short: "try" is your casual everyday word; "attempt" is its more formal, more serious cousin. When in doubt in informal conversation, "try" is fine. When writing formally or describing something genuinely difficult and significant, "attempt" fits better.

This is very important. The word "attempt" says nothing about success. It is completely neutral about the result. You must always read the rest of the sentence or context to find out what happened.

She attempted to open the lock. — Did she open it? We don't know yet.
She attempted to open the lock, but failed. — She did not open it.
She attempted to open the lock, and succeeded. — She opened it.

Without extra information, "attempted" only confirms: she made an effort. Nothing more, nothing less.

This is actually why "attempt" is such a precise word. It separates the act of trying from the result of trying — two things that are, in reality, always separate.

Because "attempt" is tied to difficulty and uncertainty, it often carries a slight feeling of courage, determination, or seriousness. When you say someone "attempted" something, you are subtly acknowledging that it was not easy, that it took effort, and that failure was a real possibility they faced.

Against all odds, she attempted to save the failing business.

This sentence carries respect for her effort, regardless of whether she ultimately saved the business.

It can also be used in a neutral or even critical tone, depending on context:

He attempted an explanation, but it only confused everyone further.

Here, "attempted" quietly signals that the explanation did not work well — it was tried, but it fell short.

• Attempt a task / attempt a question — to try to complete it, especially in a formal or academic setting.
  • Attempt a record — to try to break a record (sports, achievements).
  • Attempt an escape — to try to escape (often used in dramatic, serious, or legal contexts).
  • Attempt a smile / attempt a joke — to try to do something social or emotional, often when it doesn't come easily.
  • Attempt the impossible — to try to do something that seems cannot be done.
A Quick Summary to Tie It All Together

To attempt means to make a deliberate, conscious effort to do something — especially something difficult, risky, or uncertain — without any guarantee of success.

It is more formal than "try." It emphasizes real effort. It says nothing about whether you succeeded. And it fits best when the task has genuine difficulty or weight behind it.

The next time you see or hear "attempted," ask yourself: Who was trying? What were they trying to do? Was it hard? Did they succeed? The word "attempted" answers the first three questions on its own — the last one, you will need the context to find.
1218: "Attend" is a rich word with several meanings, but one thread ties them all together: being present — with your body, your attention, or your care. Understand that thread, and every meaning will fall into place naturally.
Meaning 1: To be physically present at something

This is by far the most common meaning. When you attend an event or place, you go there and are present.

"She attended the wedding." — She was there at the wedding.
"Thousands of people attended the concert."
"Did you attend the meeting yesterday?"

You can attend: a class, a lecture, a ceremony, a church, a conference, a funeral, a trial, a party, a university, and so on.

Two nuances worth knowing:

First, "attend" is more formal than "go to." Saying "I attended the meeting" sounds more professional than "I went to the meeting." Both mean the same thing, but "attend" carries a tone of seriousness and purpose.

Second, when you say someone attends a school, church, or institution, it usually implies regular presence — not a one-time visit. "She attends St. Mary's Church" means she goes there regularly as a member of the congregation. "He attends Oxford University" means he is an enrolled student there.
Meaning 2: "Attend to" — To give care, attention, or effort to something

When you add "to" after "attend," the meaning changes significantly. Now you are directing your focus, your care, or your effort toward something or someone. There are three closely related shades here:

a) To deal with or handle something

"I have urgent matters to attend to." — I have things I need to deal with.
"Please attend to this problem immediately." — Please handle this right away.
"He stepped out to attend to some business." — He left to take care of something.

b) To take care of a person (especially in medical, professional, or service situations)

"The doctor attended to the injured patient." — The doctor treated and cared for the patient.
"A nurse will attend to you shortly." — A nurse will come and take care of you soon.
"The hotel staff attended to every guest's needs." — The staff made sure each guest was looked after.

c) To listen or pay close attention (more formal or literary in tone)

"Please attend to what I am saying." — Pay close attention to my words.
"The students attended carefully to the instructions." — The students listened with full focus.

In formal or literary contexts, "attend" can mean to accompany, stay close to, or serve someone — usually in a role of support, service, or protection.

"The queen was attended by her ladies-in-waiting." — The ladies-in-waiting stayed near and served the queen.
"The president was attended by a team of advisors." — The advisors accompanied and supported the president.
"A physician attended the dying king." — A physician was present, caring for the king.

This meaning is rare in everyday modern speech, but you will encounter it in novels, historical texts, and formal writing. Notice that it almost always appears in the passive form: "was attended by."
Meaning 4: To come along with something (Very Formal / Literary)

In its most elevated and literary use, "attend" means that something naturally accompanies or follows something else — the way a shadow follows a person.

"Great risks attend this decision." — Great risks come with this decision.
"Success attends those who work hard." — Success follows those who work hard.
"Much suffering attended the war." — Much suffering came along with the war.

Think of this as a poetic way of saying "come with" or "be a consequence of." You will find it in formal essays, classic literature, and elevated writing — not in everyday conversation.
Grammar: The Patterns That Tell You Which Meaning Is Meant

The grammar around "attend" is a reliable guide to its meaning.

attend + noun (no "to") is used for physical presence: "attend a conference," "attend school," "attend a funeral."

attend to + noun is used for giving care, handling something, or paying attention: "attend to a patient," "attend to the problem," "attend to my words."

be attended by + noun is the formal, passive pattern meaning accompanied or served: "was attended by nurses," "was attended by her staff."

[Something] attends [something else] with an abstract subject is the literary pattern meaning comes with: "Danger attends recklessness." "Glory attended his name."

All four meanings, despite looking different on the surface, share the same heartbeat: presence, directed with intent. Whether you attend a meeting (your body is present), attend to a patient (your care is present), or attend to someone's words (your mind is present), "attend" always means showing up — fully and with purpose. Even in the literary sense, when danger attends a decision, it is always there, right alongside it.

Once you feel that core idea, the word will never confuse you again.
1219: Attendance means the fact of being present somewhere. When you physically go to a place — a school, a meeting, a concert, a church service — the act of being there is called your attendance. Think of it as the opposite of absence. If you are absent, you are not there. If you are in attendance, you are there.

The word "attendance" carries two closely related but distinct meanings, and understanding both is key.

Meaning 1: The Act or Fact of Being Present

This is the most fundamental meaning. It describes the action or reality of someone showing up to a place or event.

"Attendance at the safety training is mandatory for all employees."
"Her attendance at Sunday mass never failed."

Here, "attendance" is not about a number — it is about the fact that someone is there or is expected to be there. It answers the question: Did this person show up?

Meaning 2: The Number of People Present

"Attendance" can also refer to how many people came to a place or event. In this sense, it works almost like a count or a figure.

"The concert had an attendance of 20,000 people."
"Attendance at the match was surprisingly low."

Here, the word answers a different question: How many people showed up? This use is very common when talking about public events, sports games, exhibitions, and ceremonies.
The Third Dimension: Regularity Over Time

Beyond a single event, "attendance" is also used to describe someone's pattern or habit of showing up over a period of time. This is especially common in schools and workplaces.

"The teacher recorded each student's attendance."
"His attendance this semester has been very poor — he missed 12 days."
"She received a certificate for perfect attendance."

In this context, attendance is a kind of track record. It tells you not just whether someone came once, but how consistently they show up over days, weeks, or months.

You will very often see "attendance" used in the phrase in attendance, which simply means present at a place or event. It is a slightly more formal way of saying someone is there.

"Several world leaders were in attendance at the summit."
"The doctor was in attendance throughout the surgery."

The same word can shift meaning slightly depending on the situation, so pay attention to the context:

  • In a school setting, attendance usually refers to the record of whether students came to class each day. A teacher "takes attendance" by calling out names and marking who is there.
  • In an event or entertainment setting (sports, concerts, festivals), attendance almost always refers to the number of people who came.
  • In a workplace or formal setting, attendance refers to whether an employee or member regularly shows up to work or meetings.
  • In a legal or official setting, attendance can mean the required or compelled presence of a person (e.g., court attendance).
Common Words and Phrases That Pair with "Attendance"

Understanding which words naturally appear alongside "attendance" will help you use and recognise the word fluently:

  • Take/mark attendance — to formally record who is present (a teacher does this).
  • Attendance record — a log of how consistently someone has shown up over time.
  • Attendance rate — the percentage of time someone was present (e.g., 90% attendance rate).
  • Perfect attendance — showing up every single time without a single absence.
  • Poor/low attendance — showing up rarely, or few people coming to an event.
  • Compulsory/mandatory attendance — when showing up is not optional; it is required.
  • Record attendance — the highest number of people ever to attend a particular event.

"The stadium reported record attendance for the championship game."
"The company has a strict attendance policy."

This is a small but important point. "Attendance" is usually uncountable (no "an" or plural "attendances") when it refers to the general act or habit of being present:

✅ "Attendance is important."
✅ "Her attendance has improved."

However, it can be used in a countable sense when referring to specific, individual occasions:

✅ "The attendances at the last three games were all above 50,000."

This countable use is less common and mostly appears in formal or statistical writing.

If you want one clean mental image to anchor this word: picture a school register — a book where a teacher writes down every student's name and marks each day whether they came or not. That register is the living embodiment of the word "attendance." It captures the act of showing up, the number of people who showed up, and the pattern of showing up over time — all three core meanings of the word, in a single familiar object.
